review_text_raw:
Hello developers,

I just finished playing your game on the Switch, and I immediately bought the Steam version to add to my library. The game's atmosphere and narrative pacing really drew me in, and the background music was perfectly fitting. Because of this, I'm happy to leave a positive review, though it also left me with higher expectations.

 [spoiler]
The game is about four hours long, and playing it felt more like watching a movie. However, as a game, it offered too few choices for the player. During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!
[/spoiler]

review_text_raw:
I want to give this an honest review, because although I enjoyed it and the game does have a lot of potential, there are some setbacks to it as well.

Positives:
-The gameplay is fun and paced well. It never felt boring or slow, and the storyline was intriguing and kept me interested throughout.
-The detective work was interesting, but not too challenging. Other than [spoiler] the bomb defusing puzzle which was super annoying and convoluted out of nowhere and with a time limit that made it even worse [/spoiler] I could progress easily without feeling like it was too simple.
-The game's ui was easy to use and had nice to look at.

Negatives:
-It's well written, but really short. As you can tell from my playtime, it moved super quickly. While the story was still satisfying for the most part, it felt like it ended prematurely due to the short length. I would have liked to have seen at least a few more days worth of gameplay.
-The ending felt, to me, very unsatisfying. [spoiler] Although I'm sure, given the after credits scene, this is meant to be a cliff hanger for the next game, the way it ended just left me feeling like all the work I had done was meaningless and therefore the game had been meaningless. That's not to say the ending was all bad or should be completely changed. But, for example, if it had ended with one person being apprehended, or something similar to give some sense of conclusion, it would have been a lot better. As it is, I finished it somewhat annoyed. As if I had wasted all that effort for no reward, and an unfinished storyline. [/spoiler] This criticism is somewhat of a personal opinion, I know, but it really soured my view of the game at the end. Which was a shame, because up until that very moment I was super engrossed in the story and really enjoying it.

Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay and story right up until the final minute. So I would recommend the game, if you got it on sale or don't mind that it is very short, and you aren't put off by the thought of an abrupt ending. I think this studio did a great job producing it though and telling a story, and look forward to their next game. I only hope their next ending will feel a bit more satisfying for the player.

[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
I kind of wish Steam had a neutral option, because there are certain things about this game that are made really well. But overall I decided to get it refunded because it wasn't worth the price for me.

The "puzzles" are really more reading things in order or straight up being given the answer, and you can't even do anything with any other connections you find early on. And speaking of that, you find a LOT early on, because nearly everything is super obvious. There was only one puzzle that I genuinely was impressed with and one tool that I found really cool within another puzzle. Otherwise, the game is very linear even though it seems like it isn't, and nothing you do really matters. You can't make your own decisions or find your own connections between information. The game just walks you through each step and only allows you to do anything with that specific thing at that time.

Other than the somewhat lackluster gameplay, I personally found the ending to be extremely disappointing, because it basically answered everything you already figured out for yourself and answered nothing you didn't. The main story doesn't even really end, it just gets cut off--and in a really unrealistic way, too. It seems to be an obvious sequel setup, but in doing so it doesn't ever truly "end" this game.

The game is also very short, maybe two hours at most. Shorter even than it seems from the reviews. I wouldn't waste my money on it.

review_text_raw:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. EDIT: I've been thinking about this a lot, and I just wanted to add one more thing. You can see how I go into quite a bit of initial, just-coming-down-off-finishing-the-game detail down below if you'd like, but I'd like to quickly say here, at the start, that I think a big part of the issue was a fundamental misunderstanding of what this game was. I went into this expecting a puzzle game, but it isn't so much a puzzle game as it is a story game.
I feel it's advertised as more of a puzzle game with subtle hints at an overarching story you might be able to uncover, and indeed it does *play* like a puzzle game... until it very much becomes about following the narrative.
My feelings below still stand - including the ones after my spoiler tags - but while I don't know that I would've felt *differently* if I'd gone into this expecting something different, much of my confusion and disappointment might've been at least softened.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Overall, I was pretty disappointed with this game.
First, it was incredibly short - I had the game open for 7-ish hours... but I had dinner, fed the dogs, took a shower, yada yada, with it paused, so I'm not actually sure how long it really took. Most of the puzzles themselves weren't particularly challenging - though the mechanics were satisfying in a point-and-click, ASMR kind of way - and then one or two of the puzzles were SUPER, out-of-pocket complicated, insanely difficult, and totally out of place?? And because of the length of the game, I felt like all the mechanics I was learning, I really didn't need for very long, or often even more than once.
The writing, acting, sound design, and off-screen auditory storytelling were beautiful. Very well done; you can tell a lot of love went into it, there just... wasn't a whole lot of content.

I saw someone mention that if there were an "operator mode," that would make up for a lot of this problem, and I agree. *MILD SPOILER* Every single one of the cases were directly linked to the main story, and I think being able to enjoy some of the mechanics for longer would make it feel a little more worthwhile. Again, many of the puzzles were fairly simple, but it was still fun and satisfying in a way, and then it would also be more impactful - learning how to do the more complicated puzzles - because you'd have to use that knowledge again.

**SPOILERS FOR THE END**

The ending was incredibly dissatisfying to me. I immediately got off and looked to see if I somehow got "the bad ending" and there was another way I could've played to get "the good ending," but no. It is what it is - one and done. (I saw someone else say that if there HAD been multiple endings, that would also help with the overarching "the game is too short" issue everyone seems to be having, and I agree with that, as well.)
Some people liked the ending, but a lot of people shared the same feelings I have: if I uncover the mystery, am taking notes on the story and correctly piecing together the clues, I want to feel like I 'won' the video game... at least to a degree. But (again, **HUGE SPOILER AHEAD**) it literally doesn't matter at all. Nothing you did, none of the choices you made, mattered. The main character you played dies, every SINGLE one of your contacts/friends dies or goes missing (you cannot save them, it does not matter, and you're informed of their demise in during-credits news clippings, no less), and the only one to escape is HAL, and they're still trying to take down the big bad 30 years later (which is what fans of the ending consider the "silver lining.")
I love when games do some out-of-the-box stuff, but the whole game sets you up like you're uncovering a mystery, exposing a story, and then in the end literally not a lick of it mattered (except that HAL escaped and is still trying, which as far as I can tell, happens no matter what you, as the player, do.) It just felt very forced, and pretty pointless.
Disappointing, because again, some of the mechanics were really neat, and you can tell a lot of love was put into the storytelling aspects.

Has promise, but doesn't deliver.

Mechanically there are a handful of things that seem interesting and like you should pay attention to them that just don't go anywhere. There is no real point in taking notes because you are handed solutions to every problem without needing to look around or remember anything.

Cool, I can run programs from my terminal - [spoiler] e.g. I can call certain people if I pay attention to their IP addresses [/spoiler]. But does that come up at all after I'm shown it? No, it's a one-off to get my to type something into the terminal for vibes. Problems are not solveable outside of the linear storyline. Problems and solutions are presented to you side by side. There is no payoff for paying attention to details, because they don't go anywhere, you can't use them to figure anything out. Very much on rails, and a disappointing detective game experience. I almost thought this would go somewhere cool at the end [spoiler] and that you would continue the game as HAL and actually find out who the mysterious baddies are [/spoiler], but this too does not pay off. Just leaves me wanting more, but not in a good way; feels almost like a demo. When it was revealed [spoiler] who the mole was I was like yeah, ok, there are like 6 total people I have met who aren't dead, of course it's my sketchy friend Mike who's been acting weird. [/spoiler]

That being said, individual minigames and puzzles were genuinely fun to solve. I wish the game leaned more into the mechanics and systems they had, I think that is where they were strongest, and made it important and useful to take notes - reward paying attention to the details! Why give us a notepad if there's nothing you realistically need to write down? I wish I like this game more!

As an avid fan of narrative-driven puzzle games, I recently delved into "The Operator," developed by Bureau 81. Released on July 22, 2024, this game offers a unique experience by placing players in the role of Evan Tanner, an operator at the fictional Federal Defence Intelligence agency. Your primary task is to assist field agents by analysing evidence and providing real-time support, all from behind a computer screen.

The game's immersive design truly makes you feel like a part of a larger investigative team. The puzzles are well-crafted, requiring keen attention to detail without becoming overly frustrating. Each case you handle reveals a piece of a larger conspiracy, keeping your curiosity piqued from start to finish. The narrative is compelling, reminiscent of classic detective stories, and unfolds at a pace that keeps you engaged throughout the approximately five-hour gameplay. 


However, the game isn't without its flaws. Some plot twists are predictable, and the voice acting can be hit-or-miss at times. Additionally, while the main storyline is captivating, I found myself wishing for more side cases to further explore the game's mechanics and world. 


In conclusion, "The Operator" is a commendable addition to the narrative puzzle genre. It offers an immersive and engaging experience that is well worth your time, especially if you're a fan of detective stories and investigative gameplay. Despite its minor shortcomings, it stands out as a solid and enjoyable game.

Here's the bad news first: This game is maybe 3-4 hours long. The puzzles aren't too terribly hard to figure out and there doesn't seem to be any branching paths to the narrative. Also, the blur effect on the cutscenes could be irritating to some.

The good news: It's a well-told story that IS short, but it's surprisingly punchy. A few of the puzzles are gripping to solve and the story builds consistently with intrigue and suspense as you go. It's all organic and nothing feels out of place. The soundtrack is *superbly* done with music fitting pretty much everything you're doing. 

$14 for 3 hours is kind of a steep ask for a video game, but considering how much it is to go to a movie theater these days and spend more for *less*, your mileage may vary. Worth it on a sale, I'd wager.

Give this one a look! The ending definitely has some hints to a possible sequel and if they make one, I have faith they'll make an even longer game with more to do as this feels almost like a tech demo or a trial run. I want them to really sink in a longer story, more intrigue, more stuff to do, and give us the chance to find a better path than just one single narrative. 

Choice matters to the player and if we feel like nothing we did really changed anything on the main scenario, it can be jarring when the ending piledrives us with how things turned out despite our efforts. Food for thought, Bureau 81!

Anyways, I'm giving this a recommend. Your choice to wait for sale or not, but it's not so steep you won't enjoy yourself with a well-crafted and thought-out experience. Light on gaming, heavy on story and immersion.

I recommend it ... but with some qualifications. 

So, the presentation is excellent. Really builds a strong atmosphere of mystery. There are points when you really feel like you're an operator for a field agent uncovering a major conspiracy. The game does a very good job of doing that. Some of the puzzles took some thinking. They're not super-difficult, but they all make sense in the context of the game and there's not a lot of handholding. Overall, I like how it's all presented.

However ... what I didn't realize is that this is more visual novel than a true puzzle game. It's not a pure visual novel - there is some genuine gameplay here. And that gameplay is pretty good. But ultimately, the gameplay is to trigger the next scene. You can't really "fail" - or at least, you can't fail in a way that will affect the story.

I had believed the game to be a puzzler in the vein of Obra Dinn or Orwell. And I would say the gameplay is as good in part. But after a while, I could "see the rails" - see that at its core, it's a visual novel.

However, that's not why I was disappointed.

The bigger problem I had with the game is that I felt it was ... too short. Not in terms of game length - but in terms of the plot. It felt like it ended right when the plot was getting interesting. 

Putting spoilers on anything further:
[spoiler]Where the game ends, when the intrigue is getting intense and the identity twist is revealed ... I felt almost like that's where the real story is starting. 

Up until this point, our protagonist has just been faceless tech guy who doesn't have a role in the story - and suddenly now we understand how he ties into the conspiracy. And we also understand just what kind of terrible enemy we're up against. 

With this dramatic twist, we now understand the protagonist and his role in the story - as well as true nature and threat of the antagonist that he faces. The stakes have been made clear. The die is cast, the point of no return is reached. 

The question is, what happens now? What does our protagonist do with his new forbidden knowledge? And how can he defeat this terrible enemy?... but instead - the story unceremoniously ends right there. Not only is it kind of a bummer of an ending - but it feels like you stopped telling me this story exactly at the point where it became interesting. Right at the point where things had fully shifted from "Government Bureau Employee Simulator" to "Global Spy Conspiracy Thriller". Our agency has revealed they're evil and they betrayed us, we're gonna go rogue, and take the conspiracy down .... no, wait, actually, that's the end. [/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]It'd be like if moments after Jason Bourne realized that he was a secret agent and that assassins were trying to kill him ... he just died and the movie ended.

Or, to use a videogame equivalent - it'd be like if right when it's revealed that Doki Doki Literature Club is not actually an anime dating sim ... the game just ended.

There's no resolution. The story feels incomplete. If anything, this feels like it should be the prologue to the real plot. Like a teaser that gives us a glimpse of "OMG these guys are really bad". 

Actually, at the end, when it shifts to HAL's perspective - I thought that was where the real game was about to begin. like, "Twist, Tanner dies in the prologue! You're actually playing as HAL. How will HAL defeat the Organization?" ... But then the credits rolled.[/spoiler] 
 
[spoiler]Part of the problem was that I figured out the twist long before it was revealed. I wasn't being clever, either - it was clear from the opening cutscene that we were not playing as some anonymous rando. We are obviously someone who is involved with this conspiracy in some way. As events played out, the only possibilities were either (a) you were secretly one of the missing people or (b) you were secretly the Ghost. When it became clear you weren't the Ghost ... well, there's only one missing person who we know by name, so that must be you.[/spoiler] 
 
I will say I was thoroughly engaged up until the ending. Even when it started to become clear that the story was more on rails that I'd hoped - I didn't mind because the presentation was so good and the story had me hooked. 

But when it ended ... I felt very disappointed because I was like, "Wait, we're ending it here? That's it?"

So I guess that's my recommend. It's a very well-done experience and the devs clearly were doing something right to keep me gripped. I intended to just try the game for a bit and ended up finishing it in one setting. But it really surprised me that it ended where it did.

I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.

review_text_raw:
This review is unfortunate, because as much as I'd like to recommend the game, there's a few gripes I have with it.

First and foremost, I want to stress, this game is great and has a good hook for its plot. The mechanics it employs are varied and fun, and you do get to feel like an FBI agent working on cases alongside others. The game does a lot to nail the feel and vibe, the UI is also great and intuitive. The game's main issue isn't one singular thing, rather, it's a collection of small, minor nitpicks that ultimately end up souring the entire experience. Without trying to spoil anything, I'm going to try and summarise my complaints. 

First and foremost, the ending left me wanting. If there was an alternate ending you could achieve by using information you've gathered, it'd be one thing, but you don't get to do anything and then it just sort of ends abruptly, teasing a sequel or DLC. This is the very definition of a cliffhanger, and as such, extremely unsatisfying.

This could have been remedied if the game length was longer. But the game's barely clocking in 3 hours, you could probably beat it in 2. And, likely because of said short runtime, the game features a very small cast of characters. This unfortunately results in a somewhat predictable list of potential suspects, lessening any impacts felt from reveals that you likely saw coming.

Perhaps my biggest disappointment with how short the game was, is that the actual mechanics were unique and interesting! The puzzles were good and it introduced so many systems, one time you're analyzing chemical compounds based on formulas, another time you're disarming a bomb while given a huge manual of possibilities. And each of these varied activities happens exactly once. You spend all that time learning, understanding and mastering a skill only for it to literally not be relevant again.

This all could have perhaps been remedied by a sort of "endless mode" that generates cases and solutions, but that does not exist. And likely never will, because the game is far more focused on "immersion" as a central mechanic than gameplay. You spend a good solid 20 minutes of said 3 hours being forced to watch "immersive" unskippable cutscenes that did not need to last as long as they did. I say "immersive", because they use minimalism and only show you blurry, obfuscated imagery, which is kind of neat and saves on budget, but also means you don't even get eye candy.

Ultimately, this feels like a passion project with the wrong focus, which is a shame, because what it does right, it excels at. It's difficult to recommend this when there's games such as Cyber Manhunt 1 & 2 out that cost less and are far, far more superior in terms of value and vision. The devs are talented, and I will keep a close eye on any of their future projects, but if "The Operator 2" doesn't provide something substantially more... substantial, I can't see myself recommending that either.

review_text_raw:
My recommendation is heavily conditional. If you are into conspiracies and point-and-click games with simple puzzle elements, I would recommend this at around $10. If you don't fall into those categories, then you aren't the target demographic and I can't recommend it. Overall Operator is not a bad game - in fact, I would really like to see more content for this, or perhaps even more games like it - but it's held back by a few flaws.

First, The Good:
[list]
    [*]The setting and overall theme is great. You play as a deskbound investigator at the not-FBI, using your computer to sift through clues and work with field agents to investigate crimes. Naturally, this leads to uncovering conspiracies and shadowy organizations.
    [*]The gameplay is intuitive and accessible. You will never have to pixel-hunt for your clues; when you're inspecting a piece of evidence, the things that your gut tell you are important to the case usually are, and they're usually clickable.
    [*]The story is fun, interesting, and will keep you engaged. It references some real-world "conspiracies" that actually happened.
    [*]The gameplay loop feels fresh. I know games in this format have been done before, but it's been a while since I've seen it executed like this. I don't know of many recent games that are quite like it.
[/list]

Next, The Bad:
[list]
    [*]The puzzles are a bit simple. At times it feels like more of a visual novel than a detective/investigation game.
    [*]Many of the plot twists are predictable. The dramatic reveals towards the end of the game didn't land with me at all because I had already seen them coming way ahead of time.
    [*]Sometimes there are clues that fall into your lap a little too easily, to the point where it doesn't feel believable. The most egregious example: [spoiler]During one investigation, you find the buried body of a scientist who worked on a secret government project. The people involved with the project had him killed to keep him quiet. For some reason, they buried him in a marked grave, near the marked graves of a hundred of the project's victims, wearing his full lab coat, with his work ID showing full name and place of employment still in a cord around his neck, and with unwiped floppy disks in his pocket that contained all of his research and notes.[/spoiler]
    [*]The game is filled with anachronisms. It's supposed to be set in 1992, but it doesn't even attempt to maintain this setting. Everybody has a cell phone, which in the 90s were expensive, rare, and had very limited coverage; the computer used by main character appears to have a multi-core CPU, which didn't exist until the 2000s; and one of the early investigations involves a digital camera with a large preview screen, which also did not exist in 1992. All of this is like having a character use an iPhone in a video game about Operation Desert Storm; it can be immersion-breaking. Operator probably should have been set in the mid- to late-2000s, not 1992.
    [*]At the time of writing, there is only one ending, and it feels rushed. [spoiler]Outside of one minor detail regarding a side character, your choices don't matter.[/spoiler]
    [*]The last and most obvious drawback is probably the one you've seen mentioned in other reviews: this is a short game. It'll probably only take you around 3 hours to complete. The cynic in me wonders if this was done intentionally to get around the 2-hour Steam refund limit.
[/list]

I did enjoy my time with Operator; if you're like me, and enjoy the thought of playing detective and uncovering government conspiracies, you probably will too. Ultimately I think this is a decent game with a solid concept behind it, but the problems I listed above hold me back from recommending this unconditionally. In particular, I feel that Operator is slightly overpriced when measured against the amount of gameplay time you're likely to get out of it. This seems to be the developer's first game, so I'm hoping that they take the lessons learned from Operator and continue to improve on this formula.

review_text_raw:
A complete disappointment.

1. The gameplay is primitive and boring. Games like Cyber Manhunt or Orwell do this concept much better, in my opinion—they’re more engaging and last longer. The cutscenes drag on, and while you can see why they're there for certain moments... those moments are painfully obvious within the first hour of playing and after that, they seem redundant.
2. The story is shallow and uninteresting. The main twist is something you figure out in the first hour—[spoiler]namely, that your protagonist is Sasha Cole (thanks to the opening scene, the emphasis on Mia COLE, and the fact that your character starts hallucinating when the agent recalls her love for singing). Once you realize that, it’s immediately clear that your friend is the mole, while the "obviously" unfriendly boss is actually a good guy.[/spoiler] This one dumb decision ruins the rest of the game—there’s no wow factor, no payoff.
3. The lore? There isn’t any. Nothing is properly revealed or explained. They just threw in a bunch of medical and chemical terms and called it a day. [spoiler]Who is the Ghost? Why can he effortlessly kill trained agents? What’s the deal with the Organization? The game explains nothing—guess we’ll have to wait for a sequel instead of getting a proper, finished story.[/spoiler]
4. The ending... It left me completely deflated. [spoiler]I hate "everybody dies" endings more than anything, especially when the game tries to pretend it’s being "nonlinear."[/spoiler]
5. It’s very short. Less than three hours to finish.

review_text_raw:
This game has so much going on that I would ideally like to praise but a lot of those same things are also why I didn't really enjoy it.  On the bright side it has a very clever user interface system I like where most of the game is controlled via a "computer", the puzzles range from really easy to more complicated, and the story has some creativity going on.  It's definitely somewhat interesting, very dialogue heavy, and I would not recommend if you're not a strong reader, lover of puzzle games, or if you like a lot of scenery or environment changes.

With that said, the user interface becomes tiring to interact with very quickly.  It's hard to convey a sense of importance or immediate action when most of the puzzles really come down to clicking and having a computer "analyze" random clues.  The puzzles don't scale well in difficulty nor do they feel like they have a good payoff - any skill you learn will either be used again and again because we have to have some way to drive the game or it's a one time use - why did we bother to spend so much time reworking the wheel for no reason? (Example slight spoiler: you will never need to analyze anything other than the one sample in the game).  The instructions are lacking a lot - they have a help button that is definitely useful but there's an element of figure it out here that at times seems un-necessary.  I really don't understand not sticking to more tried and true puzzle formats particularly because they would have felt more rewarding, helped the game, and surely been easier to execute with more precision.

The story is the last complaint I'm going to throw out there.  It's interesting and I want to be invested, however, it is rushed, let down by a lot of bad music and sound interaction, and I found myself uninvested in the characters including my own character frequently.  Any story is going to ask you to slightly engage in disbelief but if you're an analytical or practical thinker there is going to come a point where you realize this is almost like a bad tv fiction.  If you're ever watched a non believable show you enjoyed - something like bones comes to mind - this is taking the worse parts of we can rush a story, analysis, evidence, data, blah blah blah but without any of the charm of why it matters.

Interesting idea but a bit of a miss on execution for me and kind of a feeling of  . . .  why did I spend time on this? lol.

review_text_raw:
Recommended (on sale)

I really enjoyed my time with The Operator, but I finished it feeling like I’d only played the first episode of a much larger game.

The story is genuinely good and kept me engaged the whole way through. Some of the plot twists are fairly predictable, but there are a few moments that genuinely caught me off guard. The problem is that just as things start to really open up… it ends. My first playthrough took around 2 hours, with maybe another hour for a second run to clean up missed achievements.

Where the game really shines is the audio. The music and sound design are fantastic, especially how the soundtrack and effects subtly shift when you uncover something important. Those moments feel great and add a lot of tension. The voice acting across the board is also strong, making the characters feel believable despite the minimal presentation.

Gameplay-wise, I had a lot of fun. There are loads of small, varied “puzzles” that all work in different ways — digging through databases, connecting information, spotting inconsistencies. Nothing ever feels repetitive, but at the same time, many mechanics are introduced, used once, and then never expanded on. It feels like groundwork being laid for systems that never get the chance to evolve.

Overall, this is a great game and absolutely worth picking up on sale to kill a few hours. At its current price point, though, it feels like it’s missing crucial length. The biggest issue is that it feels like the beginning of a story with no ending, rather than a complete experience.

I don’t regret playing it — I just wish there was more of it.

review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

Insanely good. In something of a trend started last week by my playthrough of Anger Foot, "this could have been an email, but you wrote an essay, and an excellent one at that". In other words: What could have been a simple gimmick indie that's fun and gone in one hour is turned upside down by excellent production value, which includes: great direction, engaging narrative, amazing atmosphere and voice acting. I couldn't believe how much stuff *goes on* in this game and by the end it felt like taking part in a conspiration-themed deep state thriller and not playing a puzzle solver, and that's despite spending most of the time (*most*) staring at computer screens.

I guess my only complaint is that the story is *only* good and you can see some twists coming from a mile away, but it more than makes up for that with excellent characters and being, well, engaging on a surprising level. The Operator is also not as open-ended as it seems to be, and could use a few more notable decisions or alternate endings.

Give this a go, there's much more to this title than meets the eye. Heck, if nothing else comes up this can be my personal GOTY.

review_text_raw:
Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. Or perhaps these things could be related?

Wouldn't that be convenient.

Even with all your state-of-the-art tech you'll still have to think outside the box here. And pay attention. You might not find the all-seeing eye, but a funny detail here, a reappearing pattern there, and you just might find something that you're not supposed to.

But it's a dangerous game. For you, and for whoever [i]they[/i] might see as your ally. Things might get tense. Your palms will sweat, your heart will go a little bit faster. Someone's life might be on the line. And you're the only one that picked up the phone.

Still: this little journey might have what you could call flaws. I won't tell you what they are, because I think they don't really alter the value of the experience. You're a clever person; I'm sure you can see what I mean.

(if you're not that clever, you might want to skip this one, I've seen some really funny comments on the forums from people getting stuck because they missed some stuff)

And if my words alone don't convince you, you might want to know that the (achievement-sourced) percentage of people who have beaten the game is 67%. The only game with a number higher than this is Linelith, but that's a puzzle game that can be beaten in an hour. Draw your own conclusions.

This game has an interesting premise and it has been made well. The graphics are good and the audio is top notch in my books.

But unfortunately it's... hmm, how should I say it... easy? Or not even that, hand-heldy! Like, it doesn't really let you do much anything of worth outside of one high stakes scene that is timed. But that it not what 99% of the game is.

It's kinda like this game is backwards from what you would expect from a logic puzzle game. It's the Agents or other people that call you aka the NPC's aka the game itself that do most of the detective work. And you, the player, are the computer whose job is to do the tedious work of checking. You get one single question to answer from the field agent and the answer is never that hard to find. In fact it's almost never necessary to collect and compile information as an active researcher and there's basically no need to take notes. Most of the times you just click on the right, kinda obvious document and do the thing and then answer so the plot may thiccen.

And it's not like the setting of the game, you being the computer guy helping detectives in the field means it has to be boring. There could have been more you could do. But most of the intrigue in this game comes from chat interactions, not from actual action you get to do.

Like for example, there are two things that could have been so fun to get to use as active participant, as part of a larger puzzle YOU need to solve yourself, the chemical analysis software and the bomb defusing manual, that only get one use. And also, no love for the vehicle database, just for people database. But like, just being able to do more than to just find out an answer to one question at a time, being able to take notes and to make actual deductions? Would have been fun. Think of Mainlining as an example.

Overall, I adored this game.  I struggle with this next phrase because i don't fully mean it and understand why it is the way it is... but I'm glad I bought it on sale and not full price as it's not quite worth the full price.  I mostly say this due to game length and lack of choice in endings.  I took a look and it looks like this might be a first time game from this dev, who I'm guessing is solo or very small which is VERY exciting to see if this is their freshman showing.

Things I LOVED:
-Dynamic story telling.  There was a clear storyline running through from start to finish.  Not overly convoluted, not too cliche or simple.  Were the twists a little predictable?  Maybe a few.  But that didn't take away from the impact when they hit anyway.  The pacing of those drops were excellently done.
-Style was lovely.  I REALLY dug the overall look of the game.  The various tools you got to us, the puzzles you go to solve... all from a single terminal.  It made me think of a hacking game from the early 00s of gaming sites that I loved to play over and over.
-The voice acting was excellent.  Really stellar work.
-The game itself.  It's just really enjoyable.  It was well paced, the mystery was fun, the story was easy to follow, the puzzles were a bit easy but a few had some real challenges in there.  One puzzle was a bit too much of a lateral thinking puzzle, BUT that was one of the best twists of the whole game so I can overlook it. 

Things I wish were different (not bad, just things I wanted more of):
-it's far too short.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and that was going very slow and taking my time, looking at my phone a lot and doing a few other things at the same time. (thanks ADHD)  The story telling and plot that the game is driving could easily have been a full scale game.  And I'd pay good money for it, too.  This is top notch story telling from a new dev and I hope we see more.
-Lack of use of cool tools.  You're introduced to several cool mini puzzles throughout the game like a car analyzer, a bomb diffuser, and chemical component analyzer.  All of them have robust rules and options with them.  And they're all used only once.  You gave us so many cool toys.. let us play with them!!
-No story diversity with a [spoiler] really weak and bad ending [/spoiler].  While the story they have given is lovely, your choices don't matter.  There is just that ending.  I wanted more options, i wanted to affect the story with how i played and wanted the game reward cleverness (i.e. if you found a certain name on a certain list before you were told to.)

All that being said, if you like mystery games, if you like hack style games, this is a great choice.  I am very excited to see what this dev does in the future.  If this is their first showing, we are in for some real gems in the future!!

review_text_raw:
Some interesting concepts and a fun story. Cool twist too. Most of the puzzles were relatively straightforward, but the "manual reading" one was actually pretty exciting and interesting, and the "identifying the feed" one was clever. I just could not get past the ridiculous anachronisms popping up constantly, and some very confusing internal logic.

This game takes place in 1992. Everybody has a cell phone, digital photography is commonly accessible, "zoom, enhance" is an actual mechanic. The game's FBI analogue has a database with facial recognition data of nearly everyone in the country? In 1992??? In 2025 sure, but not in 1992. Agents are constantly uploading files to your computer from their phone. At one point, confusingly, an agent apparently sends you physical floppy disks.... via his phone...? Baffling honestly. I was willing to set aside the fact that VoIP didn't exist in 1992 either, but after a while you simply cannot suspend your disbelief any further. 

HAL's "hacking" capabilities are completely inconsistent, and the justifications for why they can't hack a particular thing make no narrative sense a lot of the time. Credit where credit's due though, nothing stands out to me as anachronistic about HAL's methods at least.

There's a big narrative-UX disconnect as well. Initially I thought the "phone calls" you receive from agents are just game objects showing transcripts of audio conversations, but at one point you're instructed to *enter a code into the chat box* as though it were a terminal. So now I'm asked to believe that my computer has been *actually transcribing* phone calls automatically while people are speaking to me, and that I can use this function as a terminal. Completely ridiculous. 

This game would have made way more sense if it were set in the current year, with minimal changes to the story or mechanics, but I think the devs were just too enamoured with the retro aesthetic to let it go so they set it in the 90s anyways. 

Side note: I had annoying bug where my keybinds weren't showing up in-game, so anything where I was required to press a key just had [???] instead. Not game breaking, just annoying.

I would recommend getting this on sale.

TL;DR: This game is a 3-hour long visual novel with not-that-meaningful choices, good music and sound effects, narration, and an interesting but short linear story line. 0 replay-ability.

The nice things:

[spoiler]1. The cutscenes where the game shows you that time has passed is nice. The subtle drug-taking noises and coughing noises makes a good addition. Even though there is no real graphics here, it shows that the developers put in a lot of efforts in making the game immersive.
2. The interface and UI, especially the keyboard noises you make when you are typing, makes me reminiscent of a time when I wasn't even alive. It just feels nice to type things and click on things.
3. Narration is good, not crazy impressive, but good. That's a hard bar to pass by my standards.
4. Mechanics are nice, problem solving feels rewarding, visual and audio clues are subtle yet noticeable.[/spoiler]

The first playthrough of the game is amazing, but there are a few nick-picking things.

[spoiler]1. Agents not reacting differently when you call them by their first names instead of their last names.
2. During the first interaction with HAL, I chose to report her to my supervisor. And after the second one, I ratted her out again because I felt even if she helped me she is still wanted for good reasons. Even when I ratted her out twice, she still choose to help me with mellow tones and such. I'd expect some type of pissed-off-but-still-have-to-work-with-you type of attitude. (This can be explained with later plots but, a pissed-off reaction would've been nice, it would feel like the game recognized my choices.)
3. During the agent Andrews infiltration event, the security camera added immersion but served little to no purpose. She could complete her task no matter what, and even though we spotted for her to avoid the walking personnel, it didn't seem to matter because the guy didn't do anything when he literally saw her in the first pass.
4. I just finished my second playthrough, this game has 0 replay-ability. Everything is the same, your choices don't matter where the story goes, Tanner will always die in the end. I guess its building for a potential sequal.
5. The game teased the true identity of the Mike waaaaaay too easy. As the head of the entire secret service unit, you would go ahead and call 'your friend' during work through secured line just chatting? Also, he lied about having a wife while his files show that he is single. Meanwhile the game constantly push how weird Skinner is but they exposed the lead on Mike way too early and way too easily.[/spoiler]

Finally, if you have finished the game.
[spoiler]Can anyone tell me what 25000100193555 means? This code is written in the ALICE file in your trashbin if you open the folder before HAL gives you the code. If you open it again after HAL gives you the code it updates to the usual letter from Alice. The code doesn't open any files in the HDD, I wonder what its used for, its the only remaining mystery in this game for me.[/spoiler]

While the game has a handful of genuinely fun puzzles and some cool twists and ideas, they're presented extremely linearly, and the latter half of this 3-hour game is basically one extended cutscene.

For a price of about half the two aforementioned detective games, you get a fraction of the gameplay, and not that much more narrative.

review_text_raw:
I don't think this game is quite what I expected. It's a style of game I'd love to see more of. But while I still mostly enjoyed my time with it, I'm left wanting more.

The story itself is interesting and has enough of those classic thriller movie twist and turns to keep you engaged throughout. Role-playing the "man in the chair" is pretty fun, and you have a few moments that deliver on that promise, at least from a narrative standpoint.

After playing this through once, you'd think the game had multiple endings. You are left wondering if maybe there's some way to correct your mistakes and change the outcome. That is not the case. The ending is pretty bleak, comes pretty quickly (the game itself only being a few hours long at most), and doesn't bring the story to a proper close. I can do without a "good ending", but there's a disappointing lack of closure here.

Broadly speaking, The Operator fails to deliver on the use of "detective skills" it says you'll need in the game's description. You definitely interact with a computer and run a few faux-terminal commands, but most of the time you're just finding a name or a face by clicking the a button that Zoom-Enhances a video CSI style. It sure looks like you're doing the work, but none of it is very challenging and it all feels a little superficial.

There's maybe one section that raises the difficulty and that's because it puts you on a timer and forces you to read an instruction manual. It's the first and only challenging moment the game offers. It was actually a pretty good moment, and the game could have done with a few more scenes this.

I'd not recommend this game to fans of puzzle games who are looking for a challenge, but it's still a fun journey if you want to spend a few hours in the world of a thriller movie. Just don't expect a satisfying ending.
